answer:
**Code-switching mixes languages within the same utterance; transcription should preserve that choice.** A speaker may use one language's grammar, an English technical term, and a name written in another script. A multilingual recognizer can instead translate the whole phrase or force it into the dominant script, producing fluent text that is not the requested transcript. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04356) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.06226)

Part of the difficulty is acoustic ambiguity, and part is the decoder's language prior. A rare mixed-language phrase may be replaced with a more frequent single-language sequence. Language and task hints can help, but a hint that is too restrictive can suppress the very switching you need to capture.

**Evaluation must decide what counts as equivalent.** If two accepted scripts or transliterations represent the same spoken name, a single-reference WER can overstate the error. Use documented alternative references or a complementary transliteration-normalized score. Also retain strict checks when spelling, script, numbers, or identifiers are part of the required output.

A semantic embedding score may reward a good translation even though verbatim transcription was requested. Compare against the audio with bilingual review on difficult cases, and measure language-switch boundaries, rare terms, and hallucinations separately. Do not silently normalize away meaningful mistakes just to improve the metric. The task definition should specify whether the desired result is verbatim mixed-language text, transliteration, or translation.

**Technical details and references.**

Code-switched audio may have multiple acceptable scripts/transliterations, while a multilingual decoder's language/task token can bias output toward one script or toward translation. Training imbalance and an overly strong language prior can replace unusual mixed-language speech with more familiar text. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04356) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.06226)

Use the intended transcription task and language hints without forcing every segment into one language. Evaluate with explicitly permitted alternate references or transliteration-normalized scores, while retaining a strict score for names/numbers where script matters. Semantic embeddings can complement surface metrics but may miss negation, quantities, and hallucinations.

Audit audio-grounded errors with bilingual reviewers. A fluent translation is not a faithful transcript when the requested output is verbatim code-switched speech; keep those tasks and metrics separate.
